AI programmers of Voat: How much faster do computers need to be?

There is such a thing as a bad question. Speed doesn't determine "smartness" except within certain contexts where the solution needs to be calculated faster than competitors, but if you simply say that computers are faster, that implies that your competitor's computers are also faster. So to have to answer with the condition that computers need to be sufficiently faster than one's competitor's computers within a field where the speed of your AI being faster than your competitor's matters. Depending on your perspective, that's not really answering anything useful, but to be fair, your question isn't really asking anything useful, so it may be about as good as you're gonna get. I'm not actually an AI programmer, but I am familiar with programming and I'm vaguely familiar with a shallow level of the technical aspects of AI. I doubt you're going to get any quality replies, but if anybody wants to provide a less bullshit answer, you're certainly welcome if you don't feel like it'd be too much of a waste of your time.

Speed is not enough to solve the problem. The speed in Hz of computers is stuck at 3-5 GHZ because of quantum mechanics. What is implied by speed is development of main memory and or secondary storage with extremely low latency. We can assemble large arrays of flash memory but that too is not enough to wish AI into existence. There are classically two parts when dealing with how computers work, the data and the instructions for operations on it. Most of the speed improvements of the last 20 years have come in making the data get to the instruction pipeline as fast as possible.

An algorithm is just a way of doing things, like the "order of operations" from primary school, in essence it should not depend too much on one particular generation of computers too much. A working algorithm can be implemented in any number of ways of writing the code. The key problem is algorithms for defining what AI should do. This implies there are a series of programming statements that can produce "intelligence". All computer computations CAN be processed by hand with pencil and paper, it is only a matter of time.

Lets consider AI a programming "black box":

What are the inputs? What are the outputs? What does undefined input do? how is undefined output handled?

A computer running neural networks until it enumerates some predefined output given a set input is not exactly `"intelligence". In that case it seems little more than a giant super advanced clock tower or graphic calculator.

I was thinking about throughput speed, not just processor speed. When dealing with AI, there are scaling issues that are involved with how algorithms are designed. One algorithm may be very fast, but if in order to achieve that speed it requires unrealistic amounts of memory, then it won't be pursued. Computers for the most part need to be faster because of the size of the problems we work on. In databases there's a problem called fanning, where you are joining tables repeatedly (simplification). AI is just a tool which can produce a heuristic for solving problems. And they may potentially need more speed because training AI is a slow process.
